title: Highway Signs
alt: Highway engineers like Planck units because, like the speed of light, the energy capacity of a typical car's gas tank is 1.
transcript:
[Two highway signs stand along a road with mountains in the background. One wide sign reads "NEXT EXIT" above a number starting with 1,390 followed by around thirty-six zeroes (the propreantepenultimate and preantepenultimate zero are fully, the sixth-to-last is partly blocked by post of taller sign). A second, taller sign reads "Speed Limit" above the number 0.000000097.]

[Caption below the panel:]
Our local highway department is switching to Planck units.
explanation:
The signs on this highway apparently state things in terms of , which express things with reference to four fundamental physical constants. These may be useful in some fields of physics, but are, in most cases, impractical for everyday purposes.

In the Planck scheme, speeds are measured in terms of the speed of light, c. In this case, the speed limit of 0.000000097 c is about 105 km/h or 65 mph.

The "Next Exit" sign displays the distance in terms of the , which is considered the shortest measurable length, equal to approximately 1.616255 × 10-35 m. (Attempts to measure shorter lengths would require particles whose quantum wavelength was smaller than the Planck length and, since short wavelengths correspond to high energy, such particles would collapse into black holes before they could be used. A black hole with such a low mass would then evaporate by  in a tiny fraction of a second, in a burst of radiation and particles.) 1.39 × 1039 Planck lengths is about 23 km, or 14 miles.

It would likely be impractical for drivers to count the digits in that sign at highway speeds. If the highway department were to insist on using these units, they would be more readable (but less funny) if the numbers were in scientific notation. Of course, many drivers would find that hard to understand, too.

The title text claims that highway engineers like Planck units because the energy capacity of a gas tank is 1. The  is the mass-energy equivalent of 1 Planck mass (about 21.76 micrograms), and equal to approximately 1.956 gigajoules. On average, petrol has an energy density of approximately 46 MJ/kg or 34.2 MJ/L, so a car with a fuel tank that holds 57.2 liters (15.1 gallons) has approximately 1 Planck unit of energy.  While different cars have different sized fuel tanks, this is well within the typical range. Most other Planck units are many orders of magnitude outside the range people typically use, so it's an interesting coincidence that the very high speed and very low distance cancel out and create an amount commonly encountered in the real world.

Some cars' fuel gauges already use 1 to denote a tank's maximum volume: 0 means empty, then come fractions ¼, ½, and ¾, and then 1 means full. Of course, these numbers correspond to different real volume measurements between different makes of car. However, it is unclear why the units used to measure the capacity of individual gas tanks would matter to highway engineers, who are primarily concerned with things like cost, longevity and safety of the roads those vehicles drive on, not how they operate.

 and their advantages and disadvantages are popular discussion subjects online, though most of the discussion focuses around the various Imperial systems of measurement (such as U.S. customary units) and their enduring popularity in certain (mostly anglophone) parts of the world. This comic may be exaggerating this discourse to the point of a , introducing units more aligned with fundamental physics constants at the cost of fewer units having quantities close to those encountered in practice (only the Planck energy, while the other Planck units are overly large or small). The system also appears to lack any derived units capable of expressing a measurement in more convenient terms. Users of other systems can choose various distance units (commonly ranging from nanometers to kilometers or "thous" to miles) to match their needs. Similarly, a somewhat usable system could be derived from the Planck system by borrowing , for example "quettakilolength" (1033 Planck lengths = 1.616255 cm) or the "nano-c" (10-9 × c = 0.2998 m/s, 1.079 km/h, or 0.6706 MPH). 

Systems of measurement are a recurring topic on xkcd. 3092: Baker's Units demonstrates units which are arguably more ridiculous than the ones shown here. In 3065: Square Units, the issues with repeated unit conversion are demonstrated (similarly, in this comic, unit conversions would be necessary for most people to understand the signs). 3038: Uncanceled Units and 2292: Thermometer deal with even more unusual, but valid, units. 3164: Metric Tip presents another case of switching from one system of measurements to another.
